explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The writer says the LORD "…has clothed and armed Himself with strength." (Psalm 93:1) Notice he says clothed AND armed, so strength is both what He wears and what He carries. I can barely carry a tray of cookies without my mustache getting tangled.

Light is a good guess, friend. But here the writer says the LORD "…has clothed and armed Himself with strength." (Psalm 93:1) The verse also says He is robed in majesty. Strength is the word the writer picks for this one.

Righteousness is a big, important word, so I see why it jumped out. But the verse says the LORD "…has clothed and armed Himself with strength." (Psalm 93:1) Strength is the word the writer picks for what He wears and carries. That one is worth tucking in your apron pocket.

That's it, baker. The writer says the world "…is firmly established; it cannot be moved." (Psalm 93:1) That's a sturdy world. My bakery counter wobbles when I sneeze, and this verse is talking about something far steadier.

Counted sounds like something a person could try, I'll give you that. But the verse says the world "…is firmly established; it cannot be moved." (Psalm 93:1) The writer is talking about how steady the world is, not how many of anything there are. The word you want is moved.

Seen? I squint at my oven window all day, friend, but the writer isn't talking about eyesight. He says the world "…is firmly established; it cannot be moved." (Psalm 93:1) The point is how firmly it stands, so the word is moved.
True, friend. The writer says to the LORD, "Your throne was established long ago…" (Psalm 93:2) Verse 1 talked about Him, and now the writer says "Your." That's worth noticing.

Not quite, baker, and this one is a real true statement. The writer tells the LORD, "Your throne was established long ago; You are from all eternity." (Psalm 93:2) So the throne has been in place since long ago. It's a True one, and the psalm says it right to Him.

Right on, friend. The writer tells the LORD, "You are from all eternity." (Psalm 93:2) That's not just old. It's far bigger than anything I can compare it to, and I'm only a cookie stamper with a mustache.

Noah is a long way back, so I see the pull. But the writer tells the LORD, "You are from all eternity." (Psalm 93:2) That goes back further than any person's days. Noah's days are way too recent for this verse.

Moses, the man God sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is a great name to land on, friend. But the writer tells the LORD, "You are from all eternity." (Psalm 93:2) That reaches back past Moses and past everyone else. The verse leaves no starting line at all.
That's the one, baker. The writer says, "The floodwaters have risen, O LORD…" (Psalm 93:3) Notice he's still speaking right to the LORD. The water is getting noisy, and he says so plainly.

Nations is a fair guess when something is rising, friend. But in this verse the writer says, "The floodwaters have risen, O LORD…" (Psalm 93:3) The rivers and seas are the ones making noise here. So the word is floodwaters.

Enemies is a fair guess when something is rising up and roaring. But the verse says, "The floodwaters have risen, O LORD…" (Psalm 93:3) The text never says anything about enemies. It's all water here, so floodwaters is your word.

Yes, friend. The writer says, "Above the roar of many waters—the mighty breakers of the sea—the LORD on high is majestic." (Psalm 93:4) The loudest thing in the verse is the sea, and the writer still puts the LORD above it. I can't even out-shout my own oven timer.

The whirlwind is a place the LORD speaks from in Job 38:1, so I see why you picked it. But this psalm is about water, and it says, "Above the roar of many waters—the mighty breakers of the sea—the LORD on high is majestic." (Psalm 93:4) So the answer is on high, above the roar. No wind needed here.

Down under all that water sounds like a wet and noisy spot, baker. But the writer goes the other direction: "Above the roar of many waters—the mighty breakers of the sea—the LORD on high is majestic." (Psalm 93:4) He's on high, above the roar. Nobody's swimming in this verse.

Not this time, friend. The writer says to the LORD, "Your testimonies are fully confirmed…" (Psalm 93:5) Fully confirmed means they're already settled. So nothing is waiting to be proven, and the answer is False.

False is right, baker. The writer says to the LORD, "Your testimonies are fully confirmed…" (Psalm 93:5) Fully confirmed means there's nothing left waiting on proof. That's a solid thing to lean on, and you leaned right.

That's right, friend. The writer says, "holiness adorns Your house, O LORD…" (Psalm 93:5) Holiness is what the writer names as the house's adornment. My bakery gets sprinkles on the counter, and the writer names something better for His house.

Riches would be a natural thing to put in a grand house, I get it. But the writer says, "holiness adorns Your house, O LORD…" (Psalm 93:5) Holiness is what decorates it, and the verse names nothing else. So the answer is holiness.

Victory sounds like a fine thing to hang on a wall, baker. But the verse says, "holiness adorns Your house, O LORD…" (Psalm 93:5) The writer picks holiness, plain and simple. Victory just isn't in this verse.

explanations.answer: For all the days to come
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer says holiness adorns the LORD's house "…for all the days to come." (Psalm 93:5) That's no expiration date. My cookies can't say the same, because they go stale by the weekend. It's a lovely way to end the psalm.

The floods were the loud part of the psalm, so I see how they stuck in your head. But the writer says holiness adorns the house "…for all the days to come." (Psalm 93:5) He doesn't hang it on the floods at all. The answer is all the days to come.

explanations.answer: As long as the world stands
explanations.explanation: That's close in spirit, friend, but it's not what the writer says. He says holiness adorns the house "…for all the days to come." (Psalm 93:5) He doesn't tie it to how long the world stands. Use his exact words and you've got it.
